title: Dose-response relationship between statin therapy and glycaemia in community-based patients with type 2 diabetes: the Fremantle Diabetes Study.
text_summary: 本文围绕“Dose-response relationship between statin therapy and glycaemia in community-based patients with type 2 diabetes: the Fremantle Diabetes Study.”开展研究，具体研究方法、结果和结论见论文正文。

--- Page 1 ---

Accepted Article
Dose-response relationship between statin therapy and glycaemia in community-based 
patients with type 2 diabetes: The Fremantle Diabetes Study 
 
Running title: Statins and glycaemia in type 2 diabetes 
 
Timothy M E Davis,1 Imran Badshah,2 S A Paul Chubb,1,3,4,5 Wendy A Davis1 
 
1. School of Medicine and Pharmacology, Fremantle Hospital, PO Box 480, Fremantle, 
Western Australia 6959, Australia; 
2. Department of Endocrinology, Fiona Stanley Hospital, 102-118 Murdoch Drive, Murdoch, 
Western Australia 6150, Australia 
3. Department of Clinical Biochemistry, PathWest Laboratory Medicine WA, Royal Perth 
Hospital, GPO Box X2213, Perth, Western Australia 6847, Australia;  
4. School of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Western Australia, Nedlands, 
Western Australia 6009, Australia;  
5. Department of Clinical Biochemistry, PathWest Laboratory Medicine WA, Fiona Stanley 
Hospital, 102-118 Murdoch Drive, Murdoch, Western Australia 6150, Australia 
 
Corresponding author: Professor Timothy M E Davis, School of Medicine and 
Pharmacology, Fremantle Hospital, PO Box 480, Fremantle, Western Australia 6959, 
Australia; phone +618 9431 3229; email tim.davis@uwa.edu.au 
 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
 
 
This article has been accepted for publication and undergone full peer review but has not 
been through the copyediting, typesetting, pagination and proofreading process, which 
may lead to differences between this version and the Version of Record. Please cite this 
article as doi: 10.1111/dom.12710 
 
 

--- Page 2 ---

Accepted Article
Abstract 
Although statins may increase glycaemia in type 2 diabetes, available data are from single-
dose intervention trials or in studies with no adjustment for concomitant changes in blood 
glucose-lowering therapy. To provide real-life data covering common statin types and doses, 
HbA1c data from patients in the Fremantle Diabetes Study Phases I (FDS1) and II (FDS2) and 
on stable diabetes treatment before and after statin initiation were analysed. Intensity of statin 
therapy was categorised as low, moderate or high based on within-group dose regimens with 
similar serum LDL-cholesterol lowering effects. In pooled analyses of 335 eligible FDS1 and 
FDS2 patients, there was no change in HbA1c in the low intensity group (0.04% or 0.4 
mmol/mol; n=159, P=0.40), but a mean 0.26% (2.8 mmol/mol) increase in the moderate 
intensity group (n=185, P=0.022) and a larger mean increase of 1.05% (11.5 mmol/mol) 
increase in the high intensity group (n=11, P=0.023). These real-life data suggest a dose-
response relationship between statin treatment intensity and glycaemia that has potential 
clinical implications.  
 
 
 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

--- Page 3 ---

Accepted Article
Introduction 
Data from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) [1] and observational studies [2] suggest that 
statins increase diabetes incidence. In addition, a meta-analysis of RCT data from patients 
with pre-existing diabetes suggested a mean HbA1c increase of 0.12% (1.3 mmol/mol) in 
statin-treated versus placebo-treated patients [3]. This latter conclusion was constrained by 
non-standardised follow-up and a lack of adjustment for changes in blood glucose-lowering 
therapy, but post hoc analysis of Collaborative Atorvastatin in Diabetes Trial (CARDS) data 
addressing these limitations confirmed a similar net mean HbA1c increase of 0.14% (1.4 
mmol/mol) with 10 mg atorvastatin daily [4].  
 
Questions remain as to the glycaemic effect of statin therapy in patients with diabetes outside 
RCTs and who are taking different statin types/doses. There is weak evidence from RCTs [3] 
and clinic-based studies [5] that more potent statins have the greatest influence on glycaemia 
in diabetes, consistent with a greater risk of new diabetes in intensive-dose versus moderate-
dose statin therapy in RCTs [6]. In addition, recommendations for statin prescription 
encompass most patients at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes [7], limiting the availability of data 
from contemporary cohorts for investigation of the differential real-life effects of statin 
regimens on glycaemic control. We have, therefore, used longitudinal  observational data 
from the Fremantle Diabetes Study (FDS) [8], both Phase I (FDS1) in which patients were 
recruited between 1993 and 1996 before most major statin RCTs had reported and Phase II 
(FDS2) which recruited patients between 2008 and 2011 from the same geographical area, to 
assess whether i) statin-associated changes in glycaemic control seen in RCTs are confirmed 
in community-based, representative patients with type 2 diabetes, and ii) differences in the 
intensity of statin therapy parallel changes in glycaemia. 
 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

--- Page 4 ---

Accepted Article
Methods 
The FDS1 cohort included 1,296 patients with type 2 diabetes screened annually to 
November 2001, while the FDS2 cohort included 1,551 patients with type 2 diabetes 
followed through continuing biennial face-to-face assessments. In both Phases, any patient 
identified with diabetes from a variety of sources and resident in the study catchment area 
was eligible for recruitment. In addition to comprehensive demographic, clinical and 
laboratory data, full details of all medications were recorded at each assessment. We analysed 
data from patients in both cohorts who commenced a statin and who had an FDS assessment 
(including HbA1c measurement) either side of this therapeutic change.  
 
Statin therapy was classified as high (simvastatin/atorvastatin >40 mg/day, rosuvastatin >10 
mg/day), moderate (simvastatin >10 and ≤40 mg/day, atorvastatin ≤40 mg/day, rosuvastatin 
≤10 mg/day, pravastatin >20 mg/day, fluvastatin >40 mg/day) or low (simvastatin ≤10 
mg/day, fluvastatin ≤40 mg/day, pravastatin ≤20 mg/day) intensity, regimens within these 
groups having equivalent effects on LDL-cholesterol [9]. Lovastatin was never marketed in 
Australia and rosuvastatin became available in 2006. HbA1c was measured by high 
performance liquid chromatography in FDS1 and by immunoassay in FDS2, with a 
calibration equation standardising all levels to the FDS2 assay [10]. Changes in HbA1c over 
time were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. 
  
Results 
At baseline, 86 (6.6%) of FDS1 type 2 participants were statin-treated (see Supplementary 
Figure). During follow-up, 319 (26.3%) of the remaining 1,210 started statin treatment. 
Compared with existing statin users, initiators were more likely to be dyslipidaemic, and 
were less likely to be taking antihypertensive medications or aspirin, but had half the

--- Page 5 ---

Accepted Article
prevalence of ischaemic heart disease and lower 5-year cardiovascular risk [11] (see 
Supplementary Table). Compared with non-statin-treated patients, statin initiators were 
younger, had shorter diabetes duration, less intensive glycaemic management and a lower 
HbA1c. They had higher serum total/LDL-cholesterol, higher triglycerides, greater use of 
lipid-modifying therapy (mostly fibrates), but a similar 5-year cardiovascular risk and 
prevalence of cardiovascular disease (see Supplementary Table).  
 
Of 319 FDS1 statin initiators, 285 (89.3%) did not have their diabetes treatment intensified, 
either from diet to oral glucose-lowering medication (OGLM) or from OGLM to insulin. 
There was a significant increase in HbA1c of 0.13% (1.4 mmol/mol) over 1.3±0.9 years in 
these patients but in none of the subgroups was the change significant (see Table 1). There 
were 248 patients (77.7% of initiators) in whom blood glucose-lowering treatment was not 
intensified and the dose of statin was documented. Most (62.1%) were low intensity, 37.9% 
were medium intensity, and none were high intensity. There was no change in HbA1c in the 
low intensity group but a significant mean 0.26% (2.9 mmol/mol) increase in the moderate 
intensity group (see Table 1). 
 
At baseline, 1,030 (66.4%) of FDS2 participants were statin-treated (see Supplementary 
Figure). During follow-up, 143 (27.4%) of the remaining 521 started statin treatment. 
Compared with existing statin users, statin initiators were younger, had higher serum 
total/LDL-cholesterol, and were less likely to be taking insulin, antihypertensive medications 
or aspirin, but had a lower prevalence of ischaemic heart disease and lower 5-year 
cardiovascular risk. Compared with non-statin-treated patients, statin initiators had higher 
serum triglycerides (see Supplementary Table).

--- Page 6 ---

Accepted Article
Of the 143 FDS2 statin initiators, 112 (78.3%) did not have their diabetes treatment changed 
significantly during the 2.1±0.3 years between HbA1c measurements. There was a non-
significant HbA1c increase of 0.23% (2.5 mmol/mol) in these patients but a significant mean 
increase of 0.43% (4.6 mmol/mol) in the atorvastatin group (50.0% of patients; see Table 1). 
There were 107 (74.8% of statin initiators) in whom blood glucose-lowering treatment was 
not significantly intensified and the statin dose was documented. Most (85.0%) were medium 
intensity, 4.7% were low intensity, and 10.3% were high intensity. There was no change in 
HbA1c in the low/medium intensity groups but a significant mean 1.05% (11.5 mmol/mol) 
increase in the high intensity group (see Table 1).  
 
The changes in HbA1c by statin intensity group for pooled FDS1 and FDS2 patients are 
shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. There was no change in HbA1c in the low intensity group but 
a significant mean 0.22% (2.4 mmol/mol) increase in the moderate intensity group. Only 
FDS2 patients were in the pooled high intensity group. 
 
Conclusions 
These real-life data from representative community-based patients with type 2 diabetes 
parallel the results of RCTs in diabetes but extend the assessment of the effect of statin 
therapy on glycaemic control to the intensity of lipid-lowering treatment. We found evidence 
that low intensity statin therapy has no effect on glycaemia but that there is a graded increase 
in HbA1c with more intensive regimens. Moderate intensity statins increased the HbA1c by 
0.22% (2.4 mmol/mol) in pooled FDS1/FDS2 samples, while high intensity therapy was 
associated with a higher mean increase (1.05% or 11.5 mmol/mol). Based on ≥0.3% (≥3.3 
mmol/mol) representing a clinically significant effect [12], this suggests that patients initiated 
on high intensity statin therapy may require parallel intensification of diabetes treatment.

--- Page 7 ---

Accepted Article
 
The CARDS trial employed moderate intensity therapy (atorvastatin 10 mg daily) which was 
associated with net mean HbA1c increase of 0.14% (1.4 mmol/mol) [4] after adjustment for 
changes in diabetes treatment. This was within the 95% CI for moderate intensity statins in 
pooled FDS1/FDS2 analyses (0.06-0.38% or 0.7-4.2 mmol/mol) also after excluding 
significant intensification of blood glucose-lowering therapy. Although there was no 
allowance for diabetes treatment intensification, the meta-analysis of RCT data from patients 
with diabetes, most of whom received moderate intensity statin therapy, found a similar mean 
HbA1c increase of 0.12% (1.3 mmol/mol) [3]. Taken together, these data provide evidence 
that the initiation of low/moderate intensity statin treatment does not usually have a clinically 
meaningful impact on glycaemic control. However, data from FDS2 suggest that high 
intensity statin therapy has a greater effect. 
 
As reviewed [13], Mendelian randomization studies suggest that the effect of statins on 
glucose homeostasis reflects reduced HMG-CoA reductase activity, while there is in vitro 
and in vivo evidence that reduced synthesis of mevalonate pathway products and increased 
cholesterol loading impairs pancreatic beta cell function and decreases tissue insulin 
sensitivity. These effects are likely quantitative, consistent with the graded increase in HbA1c 
by intensity of statin therapy shown in Figure 1. Clinicians should, therefore, be aware that 
introduction of simvastatin/atorvastatin >40 mg/day or rosuvastatin >10 mg/day may lead to 
the need for more intensive treatment for diabetes depending on the current level of control 
and individualised glycaemic targets. In FDS2, high intensity statin therapy was associated 
with a change in median HbA1c from 6.6% to 8.0% (49 to 64 mmol/mol), implying that a 
substantial proportion of patients went from adequate to sub-optimal control [14]. Given the 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

--- Page 8 ---

Accepted Article
tendency to therapeutic procrastination in type 2 diabetes [15], this effect may have adverse 
consequences for chronic vascular complications. 
 
The present study had limitations. Since recent guidelines recommend relatively broad statin 
use in type 2 diabetes [7], there were relatively few initiators in FDS2 and the high intensity 
group was small. Nevertheless, this latter sub-group had a similar baseline HbA1c to the 
others and the findings were both statistically significant and consistent with evidence of a 
quantitative effect in other contexts [13]. There was a delay of up to two years between 
introduction of statin therapy and follow-up HbA1c measurement in FDS2 but CARDS data 
show that the glycaemic effect of statins is independent of treatment duration [4]. Diabetes 
treatment intensification within categories (e.g. increased OGLM doses) may have occurred 
but these would bias statin-associated HbA1c changes towards the null. 
 
In conclusion, these FDS data provide evidence of a dose-response relationship between 
statin treatment intensity and glycaemia that has potential clinical implications.
